verses.text:
My King is the King of noble heaven,
without pride, without contention,
who created the bountiful world:
my King ever-living, ever-victorious.

King above the elements, who surpasses the sun,
King above the depths of the ocean,
King in the south and north, the west and the east,
against whom no contention is made.

King who was and who is,
before the elements, before the ages,
King who lives for ever still, fair his face,
King without beginning, without end.

King who made the noble light
and the darkness with its [?]:
the one is the full day,
the other is the whole night.

King who shaped from the first matter of God
the first matter of the elements,
[?] likened to a lasting mass,
wondrous and formless.

King who shaped every element out of it,
who established them without [?] fair mystery,
both smooth and rough with colour,
both the dead and the living.

King who cut, famous and mighty,
from the first matter, finely,
the heavy, fruitful earth, a true mass [?],
whose ground is firmly set and broad.

King who shaped, no narrow fold,
within the circuit of the firmament,
the world, a shapely, solid mass,
like a goodly apple, truly round.

King who afterwards shaped a mass
closely and surely around the earth,
a course of great motion above the world, a bright triumph:
the cold and watery air.

King who sifted the noble, cold water
over the [?] of the great rocks,
from streams to the sources of rivers,
in measures of equal measure.

King who ordained eight winds,
faultless and full fair [?];
he holds four chief winds
and four fierce lesser winds.

There are four other lesser winds,
as learned authors say:
this is the truly correct number
of the winds: twelve winds.

King who fashioned the colours of the winds,
who fixed them with their graces, wholly fair,
according to their wonted courses [?],
with blendings of every varied colour.

The white, the clear purple,
the blue, the very great green,
the yellow, the red—sure the gift—
no anger seizes them when they meet.

The black, the grey, the speckled,
the dark, the hard dusky brown,
the dun: dark colours,
they are not bright and pleasant.

King who set in order over every plain
the eight fierce lesser winds;
he fashioned without [?], a shelter from harm,
the bounds of the four chief winds.

The red and the yellow together
between the white and the purple;
the green and the blue, [?],
between the dun and the bright white.

The grey and the dusky, grim and sharp,
between the dun and the jet-black;
the dark and the speckled, [?],
between the black and the purple.

Rightly was their form arranged,
their order was established,
with wise arrangements [?], without concealment,
according to stations and positions.

The twelve winds, abounding in strength,
east and west, north and south:
the King who set them in harmony holds them,
he fettered them under seven locks.

King who set them out in their stations
around the earth with many arrangements:
each two winds of them about one bright arrangement,
and a single arrangement over them all.

King who gave them their wonted arrangements,
customs without transgression [?]:
at one time, gentle calm after calm,
at another time, stormy.

King who shows the measure of the slope
from the earth to the firmament,
by which the bright span is measured,
[?] the lands.

He set seven stars on their course
from the firmament to the earth:
Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars,
the Sun, Venus, the full-fair Moon.

The King reckoned—royal the fame—
from the earth to the moon
a hundred and twenty-six miles,
which they measure in its pure extent.

That is the cold air,
[?] for motion,
whose name, [?] and sure,
is the [?] heaven of the air.

The span from the moon to the sun
the King reckoned with clear precision:
two hundred miles—great the rule—
and three, and four, and forty.

That is the noble ether,
without wind, without restless air,
whose name, not of dumb renown,
is the wondrous ethereal heaven.

Three equal measures—this is clear—
lie between the firmament and the sun;
my King strong in stars, he knew this,
he granted it to the reckoners.

That is pure Olympus,
without stirring, without motion,
by the noble tradition of the ancient sages,
whose name is the third holy heaven.

Twelve thousand—bright thunder—
and fifteen hundred miles,
fair the course of the running stars,
is that from the firmament to the earth.

The extent of the span—a swift course—
from the earth to the firmament,
that same extent, in level rows,
is from the firmament to the kingdom of heaven.

Twenty-four thousand miles
and thirty hundred miles
from here to the kingdom of heaven, a vast course,
not counting the firmament.

The extent of all that span
from the earth to the royal throne,
that is the distance from the solid earth
down to the depths of Hell.

King of every lordly, swift, red tower [?],
he himself formed the firmament,
as he was sure to do; over every plain
he shaped them out of the formless mass.

King of all the noble matter,
[?], famous and ever great;
the bright globe with its fair [?]
he divided into five zones.

Cold to the south and cold to the north,
the two temperate zones—great the triumph—
and the heated zone, it is certain,
between the two temperate ones.

King who surpasses every bright lord,
who set laws by his own will,
who made, without [?], bright,
the first form of the firmament.

As the shell is around an egg,
except that it moves with many turnings,
so is the veil of the firmament around the world,
through the ages on its everlasting course.

It casts its circling around the world
in a pleasant course with lasting light;
its size is harder to measure,
it cannot be measured across through it.

It has been divided, according to understanding,
as the authors have made known,
into twelve fair sections [?],
twelve parts facing one another.

A month's journey for the sun is each part,
according to the lofty authors;
on its course [?], bright and pure,
each year it goes round them.

In the bright firmament
there are seventy-two windows,
so that six windows shine together
in each of its parts.

There are, by the mystery of the bright King
who shaped man at his will,
[?], without hindrance [?],
shutters on every window.

A strong, sure cloak, a noble swell [?],
[?], fair and complete,
a covering of fruitfulness [?] spread
around the earth with the seas about it.

Around three heavens there are, without fault,
three heavens about them, entirely [?];
the seventh heaven, it is that
which was set right among the heavens.

It is no restful station for the host of angels,
but a right and firm revolving,
like a mill-wheel on its course,
through the ages in perpetual turning.

The firmament, of many glories,
and the seven noble stars
are on a single course, bright and pure,
since the hour they were created.

King who divided red colour over the slope—
not weak is the frame of the firmament—
in rows, in likenesses, in smooth ranks,
into twelve fixed divisions.

King over every weapon [?], over every height,
who gave a name to every single sign,
not [?], according to the law of laws,
to the twelve divisions.

The likeness of each sign, a bright course,
in the circuit of the firmament,
as the learned have established,
is named from their forms.

Aquarius, Pisces, Aries, Taurus [?],
true Gemini and Cancer,
Leo, Virgo, Libra, stinging Scorpio,
Sagittarius, Capricorn.

King who ordered them with mysteries
in their great masses,
a row of mountains [?], over every glory,
along which the sun and moon run.

Thirty days—a fitting reckoning—
with ten hours and a half,
passing through it over every height,
the sun runs in each single sign.

The pleasant sun, by the order of rule,
on the circuit of each year,
on the fifteenth of the kalends—fair the reckoning—
it is then it enters each single sign.

The sun in Aquarius—this without disgrace—
is placed in the month of January,
and in Pisces [?] brightly
it is reckoned in the month of February.

The sun in Aries—famous it is—
appears in the month of March,
and in Taurus the sun at its will
shines in the month of April.

The sun in Gemini in the month of May,
it is certain, no false word;
[?] which warms every dwelling,
in the month of June the sun is in Cancer.

The sun shines before every throng
in September in Libra;
the sun that bathes it [?]
is in Scorpio in the month of October.

Into Sagittarius the sun [?]
over every course in November;
in December—long its fame—
the sun will be in Capricorn.

Those are the twelve signs
which the Lord set upon the fair [firmament];
over every course they run beneath the world [?],
and along them the sun runs its full course.

Five things each day, to be known without fail,
are required of every learned person,
of everyone, without a stain on his face,
who is in the service of the Church:

the day of the solar month, the age of the moon,
the course of the sea without error,
the day of the week, the feasts of the pure saints,
in their proper order [?] with their movement.

King who set in rows, with [?],
in courses the paths of the stars;
as he [?] over the divisions,
he named them with their names.

Though dear to us is the half
of the many-starred firmament that is toward us,
the other half—a feast without restraint [?]—
we could not see it though we tried.

King who made [?] without rust
along the [?] of the firmament;
equally near its face appears
around the earth on every side.

King who shaped the true firmament
with its stars, not to be despised;
around the earth, without bright falsehood,
it turns from one hour to the next.

King who made a great sea
above the whole firmament;
the other sea is the sea
which [?] around the earth.

The bright King whom every prophet foretold,
Lord who built every fair grade,
who created the sun of clear form,
which lights the heaven around the earth.

King who made the noble moon
and the whole sea;
the rule which the King made for them
sets them in order, in harmony.

A sixth part of the world in every place
is the size of the moon,
and the sun, brightly,
is sixteen times the size of the earth.

King who made many creatures
under the great, vast sea;
no one can show, except my King,
their names or their number.

King who made flocks of birds
for flight [?],
wild beasts in the mountains,
herds upon the plains.

The multitude of noble creatures
and of their many great forms—
there is no one in the body who could reckon that,
except the King from holy heaven.

King who made the cold air
and the bright, red fire,
and the famous, mighty earth,
and the pure, running stream.

King who afterwards sowed the earth
with plants and with woods:
the world is full of their fragrance
and of the plenty of their many fruits.

King who has power over cold and heat,
my righteous King toward my [?],
it is he who established every station,
King beyond counting, beyond telling.

The bright King of the mysteries of grace,
who has shown us every wonder,
so that we might understand through them—a clear protection—
[?] his miracles.

There is no one among steadfast men,
among angels or archangels,
who has grasped through his own thought
the wonder that is with my King: my King is King of noble heaven.

King who made bright Heaven
with its bounds according to his will,
a choice dwelling, full of song, strong,
for the wondrous host of archangels.

Heaven with the abundance of its throng,
noble, peaceful, not cramped,
a solid, vast city from the beginning [?]:
the world is a tenth of its size.

There are three walls, without decay,
that surround Heaven:
a wall of pure green glass, fair work,
a wall of gold, a wall of purple.

A green wall without [?] on the outside,
a wall of gold against the side of the city,
and in the middle, fair in bright glory,
a great wall of pure purple.

There is there—I touch upon it—
a city bounded and equally broad;
there are in it—bright the light—
four long chief doorways.

The size of each door separately
of the four chief doors,
side to side, [?] by measure,
is a mile across each single door.

A bird of red gold upon each cross,
above its head, [?];
in each cross [?]
a great gem of precious stone.

An archangel every day—dear tidings—
with his host, from the King of Heaven,
with choral song, with clear music,
around each single cross.

There is a green before each door,
fair to approach, of fixed measure;
I liken each of them well
to the earth with its seas.

The circuit of each green separately,
with its silver [?],
with its lands of fair blossoms,
with its gleaming plants.

Though vast it may seem to you—a bright place—
the size of the wide green,
a wall of silver, of no old workmanship,
was made around each single green.

An outer court outside the wall
around the fort on every side,
with sound and peaceful dwellings
for countless thousands.

There are eight outer courts there [?],
meeting around the city;
the venerable roads [?] are no match
for the size of each outer court.

Each outer court is full of plants,
with its bronze [?];
a wall of fair, hardened clay
stands firmly around each outer court.

Twelve walls—bright thunder—
in the outer courts and in the greens,
besides the three walls outside
that are around the chief city.

Forty doors in the dwelling
of Heaven with its royal thrones:
three for each green [?],
and three for each outer court.

Four doors in front of it, outward,
of the outermost courts,
[?], abounding in rule,
with the same steps [?].

Door-leaves of silver, fair and lofty in aspect,
for each door of that green;
door-leaves of bronze, with grace,
for the doors of the outer courts.

The facing walls from the fort outward,
of all the outer courts,
are likened [?]
to the distance from the earth to the moon.

The wall of the green, as is fitting [?],
was fashioned of white bronze;
its height, vast in its splendour,
is from the earth to the bright sun.

The three walls, great their extent,
surround the chief city;
their height without fault reaches
from the earth to the firmament.

The setting of the walls outside,
around the fort, around the city:
each wall a gracious course, bright work,
each brighter [?] than the other.

The King who established them holds
the seats around the chief city;
sure are their approaches from the fort outward,
in the greens and in the outer courts.

The hosts of Adam's seed, vast their deed,
in their portions, by sure division:
clearly, according to law, each of them will reach
the place of his own seat.

Each host of them will be separately
in the outer courts and in the greens,
full of beauties, well,
in peace and in prosperity.

The saints and the virgins, with grace,
with their victories of tears [?], after the battle of tears [?],
are separated from the host outside
and brought into the great city.

The City of God with its light—
though great are its chief doors,
none go into it from the dwelling of the earth
except three kinds of people:

a person who fulfils the law of God,
a person who is a virgin in truth,
a wondrous person of repentance,
with the deed of [?] not concealed.

The saints will be summoned joyfully from outside
into the chief city—
good it will seem to them, a feast that was proclaimed—
each of them through his chief door.

The doors, of fair form, pure,
brilliant, of precious stone,
with great glories—hosts seek them—
with their door-leaves of red gold.

Three steps at each door,
fair, pure [?], measured at the side,
at each [?], a sharp ascent,
a step at each single wall.

The approach-bridges [?] of the pure doors,
a fair, bright way, of red gold;
they are [?], a bright series,
each step higher than the other.

From step to step—a sharp ascent—
smooth is the climb into the chief fort;
a fair, peaceful host, a road that reaches far,
a great thousand of hundreds of hundreds.

Around the walls, great their [?],
in the midst of the chief city,
glassy, gleaming terraces [?],
firm bridges of red gold.

There are there plains of blossoms,
ever fresh in every season,
with fruits of every beloved fruit,
with their honey-sweet scents.

There is there unfailing comfort,
there is light that never darkens,
music pure, fair, delicate,
lasting, gentle, smooth and sweet.

There is there what satisfies every host
in royal, very great Heaven:
the sound of the grades, the clear music,
the scent of the fragrant blossoms.

There are many seats, noble and whole,
there are many steady, modest choirs,
there are many hosts there, [?],
there is much music from every choir.

There are there broad pools,
the beauty of their holy [?],
bright, around which choirs sing,
pleasant, blessed, sweet to taste.

There are there slender streams
of every kind of fair liquid,
where the hosts settle, [?],
there are many bright springs.

There are there [?] slabs,
there are gilded seats,
[?] of the host who took them,
there are many royal streams.

There are many trees of the land,
many lands for choosing,
many roads upon roads, whole their variety,
many hundredfold level plains.

Much lovely music without sin
is on one plain of starry heaven,
many a [?] course, many a row of melody,
which no counting or telling can reach.

There are there, after the way, [?],
a hundred and forty-four [thousand],
before the face of the King who holds them,
after the reckoning of their rewards.

From the beginning of the world to the Judgement,
the children of Adam, whatever their speech,
could not, [?],
tell each one of their rewards.

Besides those whom he holds,
there are in heaven rewards
as many as the drops of rain, a swift sound,
or the flakes of falling snow.

The perfect throne of my gracious King
stands in the midst of the chief city;
a great hundred thousand are those its [?] holds
in the circuit of its forecourt.

Red gold was all made
for the royal throne of the King of Heaven,
the King of mysteries, who rises
above the golden walls.

The seats of the angels, with their lights,
are nearest to the chief doors;
the Archangels with their troops
are nearest to the holy angels.

The Virtues, strength over every plain,
are nearest to the Archangels;
the Powers, of divine [?],
are nearest to the Virtues.

The Principalities, gentle their [?],
are nearest to the Powers;
the Dominations, a steadfast throng,
under the [?] of the forecourt.

Wondrous the host which has all advanced
onto the forecourt of the royal throne:
holy is my great King, who has held
the Thrones with their great throngs.

The hosts of the Cherubim he set
around the royal seat;
above, beyond every one, around the bright King,
is ranged the noble host of the Seraphim.

The nine grades of heaven, holy their way,
around the King of all matter,
without [?], in the vigour of blossoms [?],
without pride, without envy.

In full ranks [?] by the King's law,
this is their true number:
seventy-two hosts, well ordered,
in each one of the grades.

The number of each host—a feast without decay—
there is no one who has known it,
unless the King knows it,
who created them out of nothing.

King noble above them all,
King of Heaven with [?],
excellent, righteous, steadfast King,
generous, royal King on his royal throne.

King who was young, King who was old long ago,
King who fashioned heaven around the bright sun,
King of all the saints, with grace,
King lovely, King fair, King comely.

King who made the pure heavenly house
for angels without transgression,
the land of the saints, of the sons of life,
a white, long, broad plain.

He arranged a seat, a noble peace,
firm upon the paths of the King's way,
a fair, pure, bounded, bright circuit
for the wondrous folk of repentance.

My King, about whom the host sings
'Sanctus Dominus Sabaoth',
fair above, a course of love,
the music of the twenty-four fair holy ones.

King who ordained the true choir
of the twenty-four fair holy ones;
fairly they sing a chant of the host:
'Sanctus Deus Sabaoth'.

Steadfast King, generous, excellent, fair,
of peace and seat, of possessions, [?],
with whom is the flock of lambs—a bright cry—
around the pure, spotless Lamb.

The bright King who ordained the Lamb
on the mountain of [?],
four thousand sons following him,
a hundred and forty, a pure course.

A bounded choir, of glorious form,
of the virgins without defilement,
they sing pure music together
following the shining Lamb.

Equally fair, equally swift, pure,
on the mountain following the Lamb,
written on their faces with grace
are their name and the name of the Father.

The King who ordained the voice
of the heavenly ones for [?],
broad, fierce and sharp—a bright place—
like the sharp wave of many waters.

Or like the voice of harps, a dear sound [?],
they sing without fault in great praise,
in [?] over every tree,
or like the great roar of thunder.

The King of the tree of life with its blossoms,
a road along which the noble grades run;
its top, its spreading on every side,
has spread over the great plain of Heaven.

On it sit the noble birds,
singing with bright grace their full music,
without decay, with choice graces,
of fruit or of leaves.

Lovely the flock of birds that holds it,
each bird, bright and good, with a hundred wings;
they sing without fault, with clear glory,
a hundred songs for each single wing.

King who made many noble dwellings,
many works lovely, right and complete;
with my precious King over every plain
is every great grade without lack.

He has seven heavens, pure strength,
without [?], without sin, fair to tell,
around the earth, abounding in fire [?],
with the name of each single heaven:

the air, the ether above every throng,
Olympus, the firmament,
the heaven of water, the heaven of the pure angels,
the heaven where the fair, renowned Lord is.

He has many wondrous throngs,
he has many dwellings without error,
he has nine grades, [?] pure,
he has a seat for each single grade.

There is the tenth grade, which holds,
without failing, the whole seed of Adam,
men [?],
with [?] the bright, fair Lord.

There is peace there, there is perfect joy,
without sorrow, without reproach,
where the hosts run [?], a stately tower,
there is lasting, everlasting life.

All the good that is with dear God
for his saints in the holy dwelling,
there is no one, after [?] the ways,
who could tell the hundredth part of it.

Lord, head of every pure grade,
[?] the throng of everlasting life,
may he save me when I leave the battle of the body,
the King who made Heaven. King who made bright Heaven.

The King who created the nine orders of heaven
as a fair and noble adornment,
in the pure glory of his bright form,
for his worship and his honour.

Three orders of them, clearly marked,
are those nearest to the earth:
the Angels, who hasten to melody,
the Archangels, and the Virtues.

The Powers, a delightful bloom,
they are the middle three orders,
with the Principalities, a glory without weakness,
and the Dominations.

The uppermost three orders of them
are in the presence of the high King:
the Thrones before the bright royal seat,
the Cherubim and the Seraphim.

The tenth order, let it be sung by you,
is the whole seed of Adam, without fail,
above the world, without peril, with the King [?]
who raised them up, my holy King.

The King who ordered the ranks
by the measures of every good gift,
by the numbers of their many fair deeds,
for their service [?] and for their honour.

Seven orders are there, noble their deeds,
fashioned after the special likeness of the high King;
theirs always, with forms that know no sorrow,
for ever, is his delight.

Two orders of them, surest in their portions,
watch over the seed of Adam
for every pure and customary errand:
the Angels and the Archangels.

The bright, pure Angels, a righteous work,
are for bearing messages at God's will;
the Archangels, without fault,
are the high messengers.

The Virtues, strong each one,
are for working bright, pure miracles;
the Powers, comely their raiment,
are excellent at governing.

The Principalities, blooming of aspect,
are for appointing fixed works [?];
the Dominations, holy of form,
are a noble host for ruling.

The Thrones, most fervent in might,
are before the royal seat of the high King;
many sing bright, unending music:
the Cherubim and the Seraphim.

Fixed and undecaying is the choir
that sings in star-fair heaven,
a bright company on the plain of the lofty stars,
the fair four-and-twenty.

The perfect hosts answer them
with their many orders,
so that this is what the host sings:
'Holy God of Sabaoth.'

The King who revealed to me, a splendid utterance,
something of the measures of the many orders,
of their rich stations full of hosts,
of their companies, of their many virtues;

of their gazing over the bright world,
above the ranks of the many-coursed stars,
their beauty greater than the sun's glow,
with nothing to match their brightness;

of their excellence, of their humility,
of their gentleness, of their unfailing harmony,
of their fair devotion without fault,
of their charity, of their mercy;

of their wholeness, a path without stint,
of their splendour, of their radiance,
of their bright, fair, pure form,
of their wondrous holy countenance;

of their peace in ordered ranks,
of their deeds, of their pure songs,
of their wondrous, lovely ways,
of their dwellings, of their many hosts.

The number of the angels in heaven,
according to our bright Lord,
is set out, a sure skill,
by spiritual revelation.

That is not their whole number, my King,
the number of their company in fair fellowship,
but only the number of the host that dwells
in the company of each archangel.

One, two, three for a while,
add two to them and it makes five;
two fives, in clear reckoning,
that is the number ten.

Two sure tens, a quick count,
go to make twenty exactly;
and three tens, they strive for renown,
that is what goes to make thirty.

After thirty, a lively showing,
I will tell you of them, O King:
four tens, by sound rules,
that is the number forty.

Five tens in order, a good course,
that is what goes to make fifty;
six tens, without [?], without more,
that is the number sixty.

Seven tens in a full seventy,
eight tens in a great eighty,
nine tens in ninety after that,
and ten tens in a pure hundred.

Ten hundreds in a thousand, a great measure,
and ten thousand in a legion;
ten legions, always, every day,
that is what goes to make a cuneus.

Ten cunei, though it be shown clearly,
that is what goes to make a mares [?];
ten mares, honour of thousands of renown,
make up, surely, a caterva.

Ten catervae, as I have heard,
go to make an exercitus;
ten exercitus, a firm course [?],
go surely to make a turba.

Ten turbae, sure the firm throngs,
that is what goes to make an agmen;
ten agmina of angels of bright order
are in the company of each archangel.

There are seven archangels in heaven
with the high King of star-bright heaven;
with each archangel, separately,
are seventy agmina of angels.

That is the ninth order,
made in holy, noble heaven,
of bright, pure angels without blemish
in the companies of the archangels.

The eight orders besides that,
God created them surely and firmly;
but save my very bright King in heaven,
there is none who has counted their number.

Let us recount, to invoke them before the King of law,
the names of the four-and-twenty bright men,
a noble throng of the hosts of angels,
of the exalted ones, of the archangels.

Gabriel, Michael, good their grasp,
Raphael, delightful Panachel,
Babichel, Raguel of great fame,

Then the river gathered every living creature that was within its bounds; all its host took shape, so that they were all around Adam.
Both prayed, Adam and the river with its many creatures; sorrowfully they raised their splendid cry to the perfect host of the nine holy ranks,
that all the ranks of the Lord might pray with them, without concealment, so that God might grant pure forgiveness to Adam, without any destruction.
They besought God, who rules the nine ranks with their array, for forgiveness for Adam here, for his peril, for his transgression.
At the prayer of His ranks, God granted full forgiveness of Adam's sin, with the dwelling of the earth and of pure, holy, noble heaven.
And afterwards He forgave his children and his races, except the one who will not do right, who goes against God's will in wrongdoing.
When the black Demon heard that forgiveness had been given to Adam: 'I will go in my own fashion, plainly, to Eve once more,'
'so that I may bring her out of the river by my cunning, so that I may set her on the road to death, so that her devotion may come to nothing by being disturbed.'
Lucifer came, swift and eager, the fierce, truly crafty wolf, like a swan, in the form of a bright angel, to Eve at the river Tigris.
The angel who had deceived her spoke to her across the stone, as though pitying her: 'O generous Eve of bright form, long have you been in the river Tigris.'
'O woman, though your form was bright, you have changed your appearance in the rough river; you have stayed here without any strength or vigour; you have killed yourself, you have ruined yourself.'
'O woman, come out, for God's sake; stay no longer in the harsh river. The glorious King has sent me on an errand; from Him I have come in pity for you.'
Then Eve came out of the river and was on the land drying herself; after that a cloud came over her, so that a lifeless swoon all but killed her.
Eve did not clearly recognize Lucifer of many shapes; it was grievous for the good woman: her mind was in doubt.
'O Eve, what is taking hold of you? You are much troubled in thought. I have come to you brightly from heaven at the command of sure, dear God.'
'Let us go out to Adam; woman, do not linger [?]; we have all prayed to dear God for forgiveness of your sins.'
Then they went boldly as far as the river Jordan, to Adam, [?], noble Eve and Lucifer.
When Adam looked out of the river at Eve and at Lucifer, trembling seized him, [?], and horror at the Devil's face filled him.
'Alas, O foolish Eve, your understanding has been deceived; the man who has come here with you on this errand is the one who deceived you in Paradise.'
'O wretched Eve, without dear understanding, what brought you out of the river Tigris, without the command of the King of law, without a pure angel to accompany you?'
When Eve heard that, the words that Adam spoke, she fell to the ground, fell into a swoon, and came close to death.
'O Lucifer, O Demon, why are you pursuing us? You have deceived us — long has it been heard — you have ruined us in Paradise.'
'Since our ties have been broken, do not follow us, Lucifer: through your contrivance we are in bondage; we do not seek your company.'
'It was not we who took your riches, or put you out of your true kingdom; it was not we who drove you into hiding, casting you out of the strongholds of heaven.'
'It was not we who took the dwellings that were yours, O unstable one! It was not we who parted you from your hosts, your music, your many triumphs.'
'It was not we who cast you into torments, away from your lands, from your great plains, so that you are in the shape of a devil forever, in everlasting pains.'
'It was not we who drove you from heaven, O restless one, for your contentiousness; it was not we who parted you from your fair work, it was not we who took your honour.'
'It was not we who took you from your lights, who brought you down from your great powers; it is you yourself, presumptuous one, who are in everlasting pain, in everlasting darkness.'
'Your rising up against the King of law truly brought you to weakness; you found great hardship through your pride, through your lack of humility.'
'Why do you seek us here, since you were cast out of Paradise? You have robbed us of our pure life; you have brought us to ruin.'
'Do you remember, O Adam, the harm I suffered on your account? My being cast from the plain of noble heaven, my being in degraded misery.'
'Do you remember, O Adam, the harm I suffered on your account? My being cast out of the company of angels into hard, mighty Hell.'
'Do you remember, O Adam, the harm I suffered on your account? My being cast beneath the trembling roar of the cauldron, into Hell of a hundred wailings.'
'Do you remember, O Adam, the harm I suffered on your account? My being cast from the kingdom of the fair Lord into the storm-shrouded land of everlasting Hell.'
'Do you remember, O Adam, the harm I suffered through you? My being in darkness without rank, in the shape of a devil, in slavery.'
'Do you remember, O Adam, the harm I suffered on your account? I have not been without storm or strife since the day you were created.'
'Wretched, O Adam, is the vengeance brought on us both because of you: your casting out from the lands of good Paradise, and mine from holy heaven.'
'I will tell you, without hasty falsehood, since I am learned in the paths of history, how plainly we were cast out of heaven, I and you, O Adam.'
'When God breathed pure breath into your body on earth, you were set apart from every firm creature on the day your soul was formed.'
'When you were brightly created in the likeness of God's form, every dear creature was told to come and honour you.'
'When God sent Michael from heaven to you before all others, O Adam, he brought you, in pure renown, to worship the Creator.'
'When you had worshipped the King of the laws of the stars, the true, mighty, radiant Lord, God offered you every swift creature forever to do you honour.'
'When God sent Michael to every place, with angels, with archangels, that they might come without delay to worship His image.'
'When God sent Michael — a bright manner — to go round the seven heavens, he brought the nine holy ranks of grace into one assembly with the true Lord.'
'Michael told me truly that I should come to worship the King, without delay, without contending in battle, so that I should be the first to come.'
'Then I came last, at the good command of Michael, and I stood in my bright splendour in the presence of the Creator.'
'The glorious King said to us: "Hear, people of the nine ranks! Render pure honour to the one made in my likeness, to Adam."'
'Michael spoke to the King a just word, without weakness: "It is right for every rank, in fair form, to honour your likeness."'
'I spoke to God, out of my pride, a fierce, very harsh word: "Is not Adam — a bright course — the youngest of all the creatures?"'
'"Is it more fitting for the elder, by order, to go and worship the younger? Rather, it is right — no dear lie — for the younger to worship the elder."'
'A third of the host spoke out plainly, both angels and archangels; they testified before all: "What Lucifer holds is true."'
'Then the voice of God said: "Hear clearly, Lucifer! The younger shall be the noble one, as long as I am exalting him."'
'"Though the people of the fair nine ranks go to honour Adam, I will not go to him — most excellent of form — since I am older in my begetting."'
'God cast me at once from heaven, through your guilt, O Adam, for my opposing thus His commands, His injunction.'
'Since we did not show bright accord nor humility toward His command, He sent us, our whole host [?], without victory into Hell.'
'O Adam, though it was on your account, we had never seen your face; through your guilt we were plainly cast from the heavens to the earth.'
'After that you remained here, after our expulsion, in Paradise; you would have prospered in every way had no change come.'
'Then I complained bitterly; strong envy entered my mind — I in painful lamentation forever, you in the sunlit lands of Paradise.'
'I told a lie, with cunning, to you yourself and to your wife, with deceit; it is well that I accomplished my desire, so that I cast you out of Paradise.'
'I tell you a firm word: whatever evil and harm I can do, in heaven and on earth hereafter, it is against you I will do it, O Adam.'
'I will bring every ill in the world upon your children, upon your race, in fierce battles, openly, in diseases, in plagues [?].'
When the two had poured out their fierce heat in their dispute, Adam rose out of the river and drove Lucifer away from them.
After that Adam was, plainly, for a year in the land of this world, with no one else, in excellent fashion, save himself alone and his one wife,
without strong fruit — a bright word — except grass, the portion of the beasts; without food, without fire, without house, without honour, without music, without clothing;
drinking water from his palm, [?] on the green herbs, in the shelter of the bright trees, in the dry caves of the earth.
Eve bore a child — fair the birth; at once he began to walk; good his guidance, skilful for his household, cutting grass for his father.
His colour was like an apple, as bright as any of the stars; lively, well-limbed, renowned, vigorous, deadly, fierce, very harsh.
'Good has God been to us, O steadfast, fair Eve! It was great wisdom on my part here that I did not kill you in my folly.'
Adam gave a name to his son: Cain, rough, bloody, strong; shame and treachery filled him, a fierce, destructive man.
When at last God took pity on Adam at his grass-cutting, the Ruler said plainly that it was time to help Adam.
God sent Michael, of pure manner, from heaven to the earth, with the virtue of every dear fruit [?], and with various seeds,
which he gave to Adam in order, to sow each seed in its own separate place, and that he might plainly instruct him in the ordering of husbandry.
He set apart for him on a pure flat stone every swift herb that comes up through the earth, and all the tools, with grace, that were strong for tilling.
And afterwards he bestowed on him every living creature that was on the earth: 'Let them serve you fully, the bad of them and the good.'
Seven years after that, plainly, Eve bore another child to Adam — fair the pledge — a son whose name was Abel.
Chosen of God, a bright increase, a just and perfect man; he was, according to dear God's ordinance, serving his parents.
'A vision has appeared to me,' said Eve to Adam: 'Abel's blood, a swift and grievous wrong, all drunk by Cain.'
'Take that to heart, my lord Adam: there is fear in my heart, in my mind, that Cain will kill Abel.'
'Woman, that shall be prevented, if it please God of sure might: they shall not be in one house together; each of them shall be in his own dwelling.'
Adam built two houses, a house for each of them apart: a house for Cain — a fair plan — and another house for Abel.
God sent bright Gabriel to tell the news to Adam: 'Cain, dark, rough, senseless, is plotting the killing of Abel.'
'But let Eve not learn from him the most wretched news, that Cain will drink his blood, for he is the very son of the Devil.'
'Let him not be troubled in mind, then, though Cain should kill Abel; he shall have a son of pure form whose name shall be dear Seth.'
It has been heard that there were born to Adam, without peril, after his transgression, seventy sons to the pair, with an equal number of daughters.
The King raised up the two sons of Adam above the very great peoples, Abel and fair Cain, with their mighty descendants.
The King who bestowed on men the world with its good treasures was pleased with Abel from the first, and was displeased with Cain.
The King whom sinful Cain, fierce in purpose, provoked in every way, never making peace with Him; after that he killed Abel.
Two hundred years — a pleasant honour — was the full span of Abel; it is no lie, as has been told of old, until he was killed by Cain.
The King said thereafter to every one of Adam's offspring that they should keep His will and not kill Cain.
Whoever under heaven kills Cain for that sin, his deed of valour shall not be accepted; sevenfold vengeance shall be brought upon him.
Then the great, radiant King set the mark of the crime upon Cain, so that the crime might not be hidden: He put a lump upon his forehead.
After that Cain was killed, without favour, one evening in the valley of Jehoshaphat, when a crooked, stiff, hard rod struck the lump that was on his forehead.
Since Cain fell there in the narrow valley of Jehoshaphat, he is in the jaws of the cauldron, fruitless, profitless.
Afterwards the King gave noble Seth to Adam in place of Abel, so that from him thereafter sprang the noble descendants of the seed of Adam.
Forty years — no lie — it is told, without harsh fear, he lived in peace, without disease, without strife, until Seth began to beget offspring.
Our bright Lord of mysteries, who existed before the first elements, called forth a body of fair clay — the King who bestowed the earth. The King who gave the fair earth.
Adam's lifetime was not short. Know it without doubt: it was nine hundred and thirty years, and certainly it was a good one.
After that a sickness came upon Adam, as misfortune comes, and his wife Eve was with him in every way, tending him.
Adam knew what was coming, and he said to fair, modest Eve: "I must part from you and from your children. Of this sickness I shall die."
"Alas before God, a clear cry," said Eve to Adam, "that you will not be here with me, and that it is not I who go first."
"Alas, it is a sad exchange," said Eve. "O Adam! I am left here wretched and weak, and you are going on before."
"O Eve of bright, pure form, set your mind entirely at rest: you will not be here long in pain after me, that is clear.
"Short is the time there has been between our creation and now, though it may seem endless [?]. You will not be in suffering, that is clear, except for nine months after me."
"Tell me without fault, husband, what is to be done with your dear body? For you are sure of your death from this, my lord, O Adam!"
"Let no one of my kind touch me with foot or hand until someone comes from God of heaven to see to my dear body.
"Leave my body, fair the manner, as it lies, undisturbed. I am sure my King will care for the noble work he made of me.
"Rise, wise Eve, and go to your cross-vigil. Send my soul from you, woman, clearly to God's right hand in holy heaven.
"The soul that God made for me, it is he who called it pure. May it go to him whole from its dwelling, in the company of a host of angels.
"Woman, I am not bold, in truth, to come before my good King [?]. May the anger he has shown, a clear course, become a drop of love and mercy.
"Beseech the noble King, Eve, that in his goodness he may come to meet me. If he does not come to my [?] himself, let Michael the archangel come swiftly."
Eve rose and threw herself on the ground with weeping and great sobbing. For the space of an hour she stayed there in grief and deep sighing.
"Have mercy on me, my King!" said Eve, fair and gentle. "Is it fitting for me, after worshipping you here, to speak in your presence?
"Great is my guilt, great my sin, though I have no path of lasting [?]. Unless you grant me forgiveness, I have no power of full, pure speech."
Wretched Eve bends her knees to the ground to speak with the King: "To you, King of heaven, I pray that Michael the soldier may come to me,
"to cleanse Adam's soul and part it from its vices, and to guide it after its going to death. Let the archangel come in his might [?]."
"Rise from the ground, Eve. Your speech has been heard very clearly: your words have reached heaven, and Michael the soldier has come to you.
"Adam's soul has left his body, O fair-formed Eve! Rise without dread, fair the knowledge, and go to your beloved and his fair face!"
After that Eve went quickly to Adam, and she found Adam, great his love, with no sign of breath.
When she did not hear Adam's voice, so fair in form, speaking to her, her reason gave way beyond measure, with long weeping and lasting sorrow.
"Eve, lift up your eyes and give us your attention. Fix your keen, clear gaze upward wholly on the heavenly ones.
"Woman, lift up your pure face to see the soul of Adam, how it is borne brightly in the keeping of the archangel."
Then Eve turned to see Adam's soul, and she saw the fair, gentle soul of Adam in Michael's company.
While Eve was watching Adam's soul, she saw a host of angels coming toward her along the ways, with choirs of song.
Before the host Eve saw seraphim, noble their movement; fair was the [?] they raised with three golden wings.
After that Eve saw, coming through the air of holy heaven, three white, bright birds of shining loveliness.
When Eve herself was looking at the birds with steady gaze, they were like the radiance of the pure sun, and she could not bear to look at them.
The singing of the holy angels was heard around Michael, with the radiance of clouds. They set themselves in ranks, with sweet sound, all around Adam's altar.
The angels sang a fitting choral song around the altar, and before every company they burned an herb whose name is ornamentum.
The strong smoke rose straight up through the air until it opened, beyond all measure, the doors of the firmament.
And God came in holiness from heaven to receive Adam's soul, the royal King above every place, and sat upon his royal throne.
Before the noble King, on a swift course, went one splendid angel of the angels with a trumpet, wise, slender, pure and bright, whose sound carried through the seven heavens.
At the voice of the horn, perfect and splendid, came the host of the nine holy orders, and their pure band stood in true array before the royal throne of the Creator.
They sing in choirs and choral songs, fairer than stars: "Blessed at every time is the High King of all things."
The whole perfect host of the holy, modest angels bowed down to the ground and prayed dear God to forgive Adam's sins.
"He is your image, my King, whom you raised up from nothing. We beseech you, clear power, by your charity, by your mercy."
After that the ruddy King swiftly sent seraphim from him, from beside the host [?], with wings of red gold,
and they took Adam's soul without [?] and baptized it in the stream of the eternal throngs, the river [?] of Acherusia.
He brought the bright, pure soul of Adam with him thus from that stream, and set it then before the face of the Creator.
There before the ruddy King Adam's soul cast itself down on the ground with fair love, and lay there for the space of three full hours.
After that the King laid his hand on the head of Adam's soul, without any rebuke, fair the tale, and handed it over to Michael.
"Do not be heedless, Michael, a clear sound, of the great cry of Adam's soul, which I set here in Paradise [?].
"Take noble Adam's bright, pure soul with its company [?], and set it in safety, without assault, in the third royal region of Paradise.
"In the third heaven," said God, "whose name is Ficconicia, let it be there without sight of pain until the time of the resurrection."
All the orders everywhere, angels and archangels alike, sweet was their pure choral song as they praised the Creator,
for the forgiveness of Adam's soul from its sins and vices, so that it was borne to Paradise without any assault.
"Here for you is the oil of mercy and the herb ornamentum: let them be put about Adam's body to cleanse it of its vices."
Three whole linen cloths, noble and fine, are wrapped about Adam's body, and it is buried carefully beside Abel's tomb.
The body of our forefather Adam, with many skilful arts, long since under the harsh bond of death and sorrow, was buried in Hebron.
Adam's body lay there under heavy weight, under firm [?], lovingly in its tomb, until the wave-roar of the Flood came.
The sea of the Flood from every plain, great was what it dug up: it took Adam's head and carried it to Jerusalem.
After that the head remained at the gate of Jerusalem; and afterwards, without sorrow, Christ's cross was planted by Adam's body.
Enos was the first who, through his grace, called on the name of God the Father; and Noah, a dear ordinance, first began the reckoning.
Never was born under heaven, of the race of Eve and Adam, a person of clay more beloved [?] than Noah son of Lamech.
Four bright men, pious in deeds and excellent, as scripture tells, were the longest-lived on any plain in the first age:
Methuselah, keen the reckoning, the beloved gem before the Flood; Noah; whole Shem, a grey warrior; and tonsured Melchizedek.
Nine hundred and sixty-eight years, no lie, without danger to his [?], courses of the stars, was the good life of Methuselah.
Five hundred years, by clear wisdom, was Noah's age when his children were born, fair their honour: Shem, Ham and Japheth.
When the Flood came, a dreadful roar, over the world and its great host, Noah's age, without concealment, was six hundred fair years.
Noah was in his ark a hundred and forty-seven days, that is certain; after the Flood, in full strength, he lived three hundred and fifty years.
Shem son of Noah lived a hundred and eighty-seven sweet years before the Flood, and after the Flood he lived five hundred and sixty-two.
Melchizedek, whom hosts would seek, whose time was in every pure victory, lived without danger a life of six hundred years.
The King who created above every share ten men of the first race, in their assemblies, with keen desires, from Adam to the Flood:
Adam, with Seth, ranks of lands; Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel; generous Jared, scores of roads; and the wondrous Enoch;
Methuselah, beloved of the hosts; and Lamech, praised in lineages; and famous Noah, who for a while floated above the waves of the Flood.
From Adam, the battle of our race, to the great cutting-off by the Flood, there were two thousand two hundred and forty years, a happy triumph.
From the Flood, destroyer of hosts, to wondrous, venerable Abram, there were nine hundred and sixty-two years, a clear track.
From Adam to noble Abram, with full and pure ranks, three thousand one hundred and eighty-four years, glorious and keen the change.
From Abram, exact without folly, until Moses came out of Egypt, no concealment of fair sense, five hundred and forty years.
From Adam, without fault of measure, until Moses crossed the Red Sea, three thousand seven hundred and eight years [?].
From Moses, a clear work, to David son of Jesse, without [?], without danger, a span of five hundred years passed.
From Adam, clear power, to David son of Jesse, four thousand one hundred and sixty-four years along the way.
From David, without danger of sorrow, to the Babylonian captivity, five hundred and sixty-nine full, lasting years.
From Adam to the captivity of Babylon, which was under princely bloom, four thousand seven hundred and forty-nine years, a deed.
From the captivity, speckled verses, until Christ came in the flesh, five hundred and sixty-six years, though every [?] (sic).
If you count from Adam, for every host, until the Son of great God was born: five thousand one hundred and ninety-six years, though [?].
From the birth of Christ, hundredfold glory, to the slaughter of the cattle by the hundred, a thousand years by the holy rule of law, less eleven years.
From Adam of the clear, glorious orders to the great slaughter of the herds, six thousand one hundred and eighty-four years, a keen, sure measure.
When the grievous vengeance came upon the herds of the many peoples, what lawful kings, on their swift course, were there at that time?
It was in the time of fair Cináed son of Máel Coluim over Alba; over Ireland, without division, was eager [?] Cináed son of Máel Coluim.
And Brian over fair Munster, Donnchad over lively Leinster, and Cathal over fair Cruachu, and Eochaid over the Ulaid.
And Fergal of the bright nobles over lively Ailech of Rígrenn, son of Conaing son of Niall of the battles, a prince-king with hosts, of the race of Eógan;
and dear Dub dá Leithe over the ranks of the race of Éremón, a sage rich in choice verses, over the walls of the [?] of the son of Alprann [?].
Otto the Younger, with lines of hosts, was son of the great Otto; at that time he was ruler over every plain for the Romans.
There were two kings, clear their lineage, over their fatherlands by the Ictian Sea: Lothair over the Franks of battles, and Edgar over the Saxons.
And Máel Coluim, of hundreds of feats, leading the bands of the land of the Britons, bright-fierce in every fair fight, the good son of Domnall son of Eógan.
In that time, a hundred deeds, the fleet of [?] was out seeking every fierce deed: the Danes from the lands of Denmark.
From then until Doom, a mighty deed, I am not anxious about what is right [?]: there is no treasure in any king that I have chosen except my holy King.
The High King of the sun, clearly it has been heard, he it is who made Paradise. He is better than every king, kingly his form, and there is no end to his life. Adam's lifetime was not short.

The King who spoke to the race of Seth, that they should keep his deeds with equal strength, without any union outside their house with the hateful race of Cain. Without [?], beyond his command, beyond the precepts of the King who created them, by a bright, radiant rule, without friendship with the race of Cain:
"Without exchange of rich treasures, without lying together, without marriage, without joining of roof-pole or corner, as long as you are among the throng of the world."
After a while the race of Seth and the race of Cain joined together, and afterwards they begot mighty men and strong champions.
The race of Cain and the race of Seth united with equal strength, until they went beyond every command to the worship of idols and images.
Their offspring came to hate stern God without [?], so that he resolved, because of their deeds, to bring them under heavy vengeance.

The King with the grace of kingship over throngs, against whom neither battle nor combat can be waged, fair in holiness, gentle his [?]; better than every king is the King who spoke. The King who spoke to the race of Seth.
The King spoke a noble word to Noah, a perfect ordinance: "The race of Seth have gone against my will by marrying with the race of Cain.
"Though they were pure, they have mingled with the hateful race of Cain. They have offended me in every way: woe is me that I begot them.
"Since they have gone beyond my command to the race of Cain, a hundred idols [?], I will let loose over the face of the world, a heavy, strong stream, the wave-roar of the Flood.
"I will destroy the race of Adam entirely, to the edges of the strong, lasting world. I will bring them all to death, from the sun's rising to its setting.
"Except Noah and the eight of his household, I will leave none of the race of Adam alive [?], except the wonderful man Enoch."
The great King who created every dwelling, who was before his angels, for every king [?] without ugly question, is the King who spoke the word. The King spoke a noble word.
"Hear, famous Noah, without sorrow: a heavy, strong Flood will come. Let a vast, unbreakable vessel be built by you to hold ranks of hosts.
"Well-shaped and serviceable afterwards [?], of the wood of Lebanon, lines of planks, three-tiered, strong and very great.
"Fifty cubits, no unseemly work, in the lowest storey; forty in the middle, and thirty in the topmost.
"Four compartments in the ark, a track from keel to ridge-pole, with noble rows of six through its bloom [?], with spaces of one cubit [?].
"Keep without weariness, without fault, its measurements without error: its length, its breadth, a clear account, both low and high.
"Fifty cubits, a work without folly, in its breadth, without false cleverness; three hundred cubits, pure power, shall be the length of its keel.
"Thirty proper cubits, without concealment, in its height in even rows, against the streams that pour from holy heaven; and its door in its side.
"A window, by swift measure, for light and for looking out, in its height by my command, with no excess but one cubit.
"Many wonderful, perfect dwellings, a fair, pure work to tell of, in fitting rows of ranks, with as many beds as there are couples."
The King who gave command concerning every victory, who hated red kin-slaying — it was no mere prince who uttered that sound — said into his ears, "Hear." "Hear, famous Noah, without sorrow."
The King spoke to modest Noah: "Go into the perfectly sound vessel, you and your three sons only, and your four fair wives."
Percoba, fairer than any raven, was the wife of Noah son of Lamech; the wives of his three sons, a clear work, were Olla, Oliva and Olivana.
Noah son of Lamech had six children, fair their honour: three good sons, thousands of days, and three daughters.
Shem was the noble eldest, a clear line, of the comely children; and with each son, alike in beauty, a daughter was born.
Olla was the wife of Shem, noble in her nature; Oliva the wife of fair, modest Ham; Olivana, [?], the youngest, was the wife of Japheth.
The King drove into Noah's ark at one time — no small host — a pair of every animal of all that sea and land contained.
In its dwellings, without disgrace, there was a great host of couples, with their provisions, a clear company, and their proper food.
When the perfect ark was filled, vengeance came upon its surroundings. The truth is told, by clear power: it was the word of the King who spoke. The King spoke to modest Noah.
The King let loose a swimming torrent to destroy the race of Adam, except only four men and their four wives,
and Enoch of pure devotion, as scripture tells, alone from wave to wave, like any light bird.
The streams poured down from heaven and burst up through the earth: a deluge on them, a clear desire, for forty days and nights.
The height of the Flood from the ground, as fair, modest scripture tells, was fifteen full cubits, without concealment, above the mountains.
When every creature is destroyed, as scripture tells, that is as far as the flame of the Day of Judgement will reach.
Whatever lived that God had created in fair form, the Flood drowned it, except what the one boat held.

The King of modest heaven, a clear ordinance, the King who rules ebb and flood, high above every might and every spoil, nobler than every king is the King who let it loose. The King let loose a swimming torrent.
The noble King clearly saved Noah with his household for a hundred and forty grievous days, while he was under the waves of the Flood.
After that the strong-walled, destroying Flood began to go back, and Noah noticed that the sea had begun to ebb.
Noah sends a messenger from him, the [?], swift-going raven, to see whether it might find mountain or valley or land on which to rest.
When the raven found its own food out on a rock, on a mountain, on [?], it did not come back again with clear tidings.
When Noah lost hope there of the black, [?] raven, he himself, an excellent deed, then sent the dove out to them.
A King without ugliness, without [?], without assault; no part of the world is neglected by him; his house is not narrow, fair is his [?]; the noble King who saved him. The noble King clearly saved.
Noah sent the pure dove out from him over the vast sea-flood, a keen errand, to see whether it might find firm, fruitful, dry land.
The dove makes a bright circuit, after command, after bidding, and came back to the ark without deceit: it had found no place to rest.
Noah stretched out his hand to meet the fair, modest dove and brought it in to him from outside, a clear manner, so that it was inside the ark.
After that Noah spent a week without sight or view of the lasting world, nothing but a wall of sea, no country or land of any people.
