the King who through grace chose. The King who through grace chose long ago.

In the second year — a pleasing account —
after the bitter famine had set in,
the children of Jacob went — it was a just deed —
to buy food in the land of Egypt.

They travelled over rough wild places [?],
through the wondrous lands of Egypt,
on the track of the host — sad the [?] —
to the people where the high king was.

Dejection filled them, grief seized them,
having gone from their own land,
without knowledge of the way, without a guide,
without the language, in unknown lands.

They were anxious on their journeys
because of their rash deeds, their foolish ways,
before the hosts from every plain:
wretched, sorrowful, tearful.

Their spirits were dejected;
[?] bound them under [?],
with no one to bring them — it was a question for them —
to the vice-king of noble [?].

They went through the middle of the host,
grimy [?], so pitiful;
they took their stand — excellent and true —
in the presence of the high king.

He sent an urgent messenger
to meet them, [?], quickly,
as he recognised — a just deed —
the venerable vice-king of Egypt.

The men threw themselves down at his feet,
they bent their knees in reverence,
they bowed [?]
before his face, in his presence.

Joseph asked them — it was clearly heard —
with glory, without [?]:
"Tell, hard men, your cry:
where are you from, or where have you come from?"

"What are you seeking in our [?] land,
without [?], without true knowledge,
without the language [?],
like a swift band of spies?"

"Or a band of traitors against [?] houses,
who go from city to city,
without a letter with you, [?],
without messages from king or overlord?"

"You look to me here like nothing
but base spies,
or mountain men who break the law,
or liars at their lying."

"We are all brothers [?],
the number of our company and our gathering,
herding our father's [flocks] [?];
we have another brother, our youngest."

"If that is true, [?],
for you descendants of Abraham,
give a clear hostage from among you
as a pledge that you will come again."

"When you come back [?],
if your younger brother comes with you,
you will have your hostage back,
and your wish will be done."

Before they set off on their way
to their land with their merchandise,
into the hand of the vice-king, as a pledge,
they gave Issachar.

Joseph said — a story without doubt:
"I will always work for your lasting good,
every time you come to me,
for the sake of the God of Abraham."

Then they went to their land,
as he had [?] them, without contempt;
they brought [?]
a gift for God to Jacob [?].

Then they reached their house,
noble, safe, and cheerful;
good came to them, under pure glory,
a prince of plenty, in the second year. In the second year, a pleasing account.

Noble Jacob gave thanks
to his Lord — it was a complete deed —
that his children had found, pure and true and right,
a welcome from the vice-king of Egypt.

As he had led them with gentle dealings
through vast unknown lands,
had nourished them without [?] from every plain,
and set them on an excellent path,

As he had brought them back, [?],
from every wall, with their great [?],
their coming home thankful to their house —
he gave thanks to his King. Noble Jacob gave thanks.
The wonderful sons of Jacob made a fitting plan: to go once more along the road into the land of Egypt.
They went along safe paths, with no fear of a fighting band; they journeyed strongly [?] across every land until they came to the high king.
With the high king they found a great welcome, ample and true; as right reason would wish, they were able to buy at once.
Joseph took a pure cup and placed it in the hand of a man of his household: “Put it in the sacks of the Canaanites, as I instruct, to bring them to judgement.”
Not sadly did they set off for their land, nor had they displeased the high king; as had been granted them on every journey, their blessing rested upon Joseph.
When the companies were out on the plain, about a mile from the city, he sent a fierce, swift band to seize them. That was no shameful act.
They were not on guard against pursuit. They were quickly surrounded and brought roughly from the plain back to the city.
They were brought back with all they had, bound in fetters. Pitiful and powerless was their plight until they stood before the high king.
The king called out to them and said to them at once: “Sad is the fate of your fine company, all of you taken for theft.
“For the theft is yours beyond dispute. That is no pleasant matter. Your crime brings you no glory, I tell you: every last man of you will hang.”
“O faultless king of Egypt, who have dealt with us for our full good, it is no glory to your triumph or your fame to hang wretched men who are guiltless.
“We do not know, though it may be a sin under the sun, and hard and heavy for Benjamin; a stupor as of the drunken dead has struck us down over this cup.
“We swear by every treasure, by the shelter of right, before your face, O king of Egypt, and before the witnesses of God, that we are innocent of the crime of this cup.”
“For your lives, give me a wondrous hostage from among you: your youngest brother himself, whose name is Benjamin.
“Go off along your swift [?] paths and leave Benjamin, since it was with him that the cup of Egypt was found. That is the clear point at issue.”
“The youngest of the family, a man true [?], whose deeds are bright, is the dearest of all our company to our father Jacob.
“We ask one thing of you, O king of Egypt, if it does not displease you: though you keep us at your will, set Benjamin free.
“If anyone under the green sky has ever died of grief, and that is a cruel thing, Jacob himself will die lamenting Benjamin.”
“O sons of noble Jacob, [?] of the race of Abraham, you have fallen into guilt, with no glorious help and no fame at all.”
Feebly they told their tale and knelt before the high king: “We swear boldly by God that we are clear of this crime.”
“Make your confession without weakness, a firm word before the draught of death. Declare against whoever it may be the rash violence: you have done a most terrible deed.”
“Though the vengeance of God be fierce and wrathful, it suits us well for our crooked days. It is right that we should perish utterly in punishment for the one we seized.
“We overwhelmed him, and it was a wretched deed. We grieved Jacob. We ruined a dear one of our own household; we sold our only brother.
“Our crime greatly increases our doom; we are not innocent, that we should be set free. Let us go to our death, and that is the plain truth: let us go under the sharp-edged sword.”
“It would not be right for me to destroy you. Long have you been in danger. The help of God has come to your aid, O wondrous race of Jacob!
“May our meeting bring victory, O pure descendants of Abraham! There is no forbidden deed here, to put it briefly: it is I whom you sold.”
They were struck with wonder at once and gave thanks for their meeting. They wept as was fitting in their lamenting; they wept for their great joy.
“Set out boldly; no harm will come to you. Go and fetch Jacob, without grief. Wide is your right, and strong your power in Egypt.”
It was the King who afterwards brought Jacob from the north with his sons, when they went south on their journey to Egypt in Joseph's name.
Then they came south to live near Joseph, and the best of every dwelling Joseph gave to his brothers.
Jacob lived without anxiety in the lands of Egypt, together with his family in their renown, for seventy-two years. It was a just thing.
Great is the love from of old of him who brought Abraham out of Chaldea. It was he who rightly granted them what they had done. They made a fitting plan.
Then noble Joseph died. They had no freedom and no free rank: the men of Egypt, for all their malice, put them under heavy bondage.
They enslaved them to their will after the death of wondrous Joseph. Such bondage, so plain a burden, had never befallen the world.
Many of the race were born to the host of Israel, and it was a sorry tale: with a cry [?], they would cut the right eyes out of their heads.
Much evil of every kind, which was not right, they suffered under the host of Egypt. No bondage could be harsher: they would kill their firstborn.
Though the bondage that came upon them was heavy, their God was helping them: the more the hosts oppressed them, the more they increased every single hour.
Joseph, son of noble Jacob, son of Isaac, son of Abraham, spent ten score years in Egypt, keeping to the rules of the law.
He went to his rest [?], along the path of the ancients, wise and noble and dear. He left two sons, good in their grace: Manasseh and Ephraim.
They held every authority, and the men of Egypt served them, in their triumph, their wealth and their honour, until the hour when Joseph died. Then noble Joseph died.
Moses was born, a bright occasion, in the time of the heavy bondage. Fair as his form was, he was cast out into the stream of the Nile to drown.
Thermuthis found him, and it was a just deed: the daughter of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, at the river as she washed her hands, a fair, modest, steady woman, bright and seemly.
Then she ordered her women to bring the little boy of pure form out of the shallows, for God had put it in her mind.
After that Thermuthis loved him as anyone loves an only child, and she ordered, a fine deed, that he be given the best of good fostering.
Then he grew until he was strong. He turned to the race of the sons of Israel, and he declared openly [?] before every clan that he was not the son of Pharaoh's daughter.
Jesus, free of sorrow, of pure renown, who had no mighty earthly father, gladdened every lord with a bright deed in the time when he was born. Moses was born, a bright occasion.
One day on the plain he came upon two men quarrelling: one was of his own true race, the other was of Egypt.
Then he recognized the man of the race of Israel, who was not the stronger. This was the harsh, unlawful deed: he killed the man of Egypt.
The people knew well the man whom Moses had killed. As openly as it was done, it was duly reported to the king of Egypt.
Pharaoh duly proclaimed to the wondrous men of Egypt that Moses should have shelter nowhere, but only death or banishment.
Moses set out on a journey, fleeing before the host of Egypt, across lands, along valley paths, until he came upon the maidens.
On the plain he found a great company of lads and girls, driving sheep in order to a well and a spring.
As the strong herdsmen hurried about the slopes of Mount Horeb, great was their clamour on the plain as they drew water for their sheep.
Moses, of bright bearing, sat down by the side of the road, anxious and weary, with little strength, alone, endlessly wandering.

Moses was mighty in every gathering of the race of the children of Abraham. No bright song of clever deeds conceals it: it was by the will of God that it came about. One day on the plain he came upon.
There, fair and gentle, with their sheep, hard pressed in the midst of the famous crowd, were two daughters of the chief priest.
Then one of the daughters said to Moses, of pure bearing: “Why do you not help us, as a true protector, young man there from Egypt?
“We have no strong man with us; we are alone in great distress. Around the cold water the crowd is mistreating us in every way.”
Moses rose, of bright bearing, and it was no madman's rising, and gave strong, swift help to the daughters of the priest.
They invited Moses, wondrous in every field of arms, to their house, and told their tidings to their father, holding nothing back.
The priest, of famous wisdom, welcomed Moses for his form, for his pure good sense, and for the help he gave his daughters.
Then the priest kept him in fellowship, in the one household, and by the King's command, a happy turn, he gave him his eldest daughter.
As son-in-law of the priest, without sorrow, in the woods of Mount Horeb, Moses, of bright bearing, spent a third part of his lifetime.

Holy King of heaven, strength of every host, fair pillar without fault, of everlasting victory, King of the proud world, without betrayal, who ordained them as they were. They were there, fair and gentle.
One day Moses was out on Mount Horeb with his sheep, when the King who blazes like fire appeared to him.
The King commanded the wondrous son, Moses, and said to him, a just onset: “It is better for you to go to Egypt.”
Moses said, a bright deed: “I will not go at your bidding. I know myself, and it is a sound reason, that I am a man at enmity with Pharaoh.”
“Go on the journey at my word to fetch the host in Egypt. You will be hallowed before every family; you will be saved from Pharaoh.
“You will take a sign from me with you. It will save you from overwhelming force, so that nothing whole under heaven can come against your purpose.”
He gained much victory without betrayal, much perfect wisdom with full grace, and pride; great and bright was the wisdom Moses gained one day. One day Moses was out.
The King for whom the bush blazed, a royal tale, gave a smooth [?] rod into the hand of Moses son of Amram, in a royal mystery on Mount Horeb.
The King who boldly told Moses to show his hand: one time it was leprous, the other time it was wholly clean.
The King who gave this along with it to Moses son of Amram, saying thus, a stately rule: “I will always help you.”
The King who sent to the aid of the children of delightful Jacob one to do battle, with the word of dear God, against Pharaoh and his druids.
The King who sent Moses on the journey to Pharaoh, to the king of Egypt, that he should let the wondrous children of Israel go from him without grief.
“If he does not quickly let go the sons of Israel, in the full number of their tribes, I will send great vengeance upon him and take them from him by force.”
The King under whom are all the hosts, he is our pillar of red gold; he follows no crooked way, no falsehood, no doubt; the King who gave him the smooth rod. The King gave a smooth rod.
Then Moses said to Pharaoh before every family: “Look after your own hosts apart; let the people of the Lord go from you.”
Pharaoh said, in a clear voice, that he would not give them their freedom until it was known who was greater in power, their God or the god of Egypt.
The king's druids, with shameless spells of falsehood, quickly make serpents for the prince; they shaped their likeness out of their rods.
Moses, of dear bearing, in the name of the King of heaven and by the word of God, before the princes, made his rod into a bright serpent.
Moses' serpent, attacking in battle the serpents of the druids inside the house before the king, devoured them to the last morsel.
Moses took the serpent from the floor before the full house and shook it, and it turned into a rod in the sight of the crowd. It was a great marvel.
Moses, a diadem above the ships [?] of the world, descendant of Jacob son of Isaac, pure in his speech, bright in his deeds: it was by the will of God that he spoke. Moses said before every family.
Pharaoh was afraid, and after that he said to Moses: “I am content that they should go on the journey, if the people of Egypt are content.”
Moses went from the house, from the dwelling of haughty Pharaoh, and told the tidings plainly to the good men of Israel.
When Moses had left him, Pharaoh summoned the great host to him and laid every harsh rule upon them in earnest; pride and madness filled him.
Pharaoh said, without denial, to his clans and his peoples: “Upon the peoples of God, a clear proclamation, lay every increase of bondage.”
The wretched people were bitter with Moses for his urging: “Only more labour and oppression; we have found no help at all.”
Moses said to them triumphantly: “Do not be foolish and sad-mouthed. God's ordinance, nearest in every part [?], will be stronger than Pharaoh's boast.”
The high king of Egypt, of many deeds, a false, murderous, harsh and fierce king, a bull of envy for strife and battle: while he was alive he was afraid. Pharaoh was afraid.
The King said to Moses firmly: “Tell the people of Israel, a bright command, that every single household is to make a lamb for sacrifice.
“That lamb is to be a male, a year old, without a black or dark spot. Roast it on embers in every way, and break none of its bones.
“Prepare the spotless lamb to sacrifice in every place. Eat it indoors, none of it outside: its feet, its head and its entrails.
“If those inside, a bright command, are not enough people to eat it, let someone from their band come in from outside, each of you in his [?].
“With bitter herbs of lettuce, a bright command, with unleavened bread, staffs in hand, [?], belts girded around you.
“Eat it standing, so; put its blood on your doorposts. Its remnant, the leftovers set apart, you must burn in the fire.
“Let this always be done by everyone in every house, a custom to be practised, in remembrance of your deliverance from Egypt.”
The seas ebb at the bidding of the great King of holy, noble heaven. He brought great vengeance on mortal flesh; he prevailed, the King who spoke. The King said to Moses firmly.
The King brought great and heavy vengeance for the oppression of the sons of Israel: it was a burst of thunder over every plain, upon Pharaoh and his peoples.
Frogs, locusts in bright array, flies, beasts, spotted plague [?], boils, a weak stream of blood, darkness, fire and thunder.
The plague of all the firstborn, both of beast and of man; the weeping of every house, a just deed, was heard by the men of Egypt.

The King brought the ten plagues upon them in the hour of their boasting. No weakling was he who justly waged the battle, the King who brought great vengeance. The King brought great and heavy vengeance.
They let them go free from them, in their troops and in their great hosts, and so they set out on their journey along the wondrous roads of Egypt.
Four hundred and thirty years was the bondage, a heavy subjection, that the renowned race of Israel endured in dark Egypt.
After that they parted from the bondage of Egypt, with all its malice, after four hundred and thirty years, by the rule of grace.
They made their way, a victorious company, without fear, north-east out of Egypt, without delay, and it was well for the host, to Rameses and to Succoth.
The King [?] who brought them by his might out of the harsh bondage of Egypt set a cloud about them by day and a pillar of fire every night.
The fire burned the host of Egypt in the cold night; the cloud was dark for them by day, so that their chariots were broken.
Then the whole host of the men of Egypt said to Pharaoh: “Let us turn back without grief; let us let the race of Israel go from us.
“The God who is best for ever has brought ruin on our great host. He is fighting strongly on behalf of the race of Israel.”
Pharaoh said to them in anger: “We will not let them go [?] until we bring them back with us into captivity, along with our gold and our silver.”
Pharaoh went with his host after them to the very great Red Sea; the hosts pressed on before him [?], and Pharaoh in hot pursuit.
The King who then saved them from Pharaoh and his troops brought them straight on through the midst of the Red Sea.
The great sea, of a thousand tales, through which God brought the race of Israel: the King of the sun poured it, undivided, over the shoulders of Pharaoh's band.
At that time Gaedel was [?] in Egypt; Scota, the honoured daughter of Pharaoh, was given away before every family.
Gaedel triumphantly refused to go after the host, for he was a seer, clear in his tidings, from fear of the God of the sons of Israel.
After that Gaedel Glas went in ships on the broad, fierce sea; he set out upon the slow sea for fear of Pharaoh's anger.
Fair Gaedel with his triumph then went past India to the north-east, and took land, with a bright clamour, on the island of Taprobane.
From the island of Taprobane he went, [?], for a time to the north-west, and for a number of years he dwelt in the woods in the regions of the Caspian.
There were drowned there, by exact count, of the good men of Egypt, five hundred glorious kings [?] around the high king, around Pharaoh.
As for the rest of the host besides these, no one knows their number: no one in any generation could determine the count of their many thousands.
The King who let loose the red Red Sea upon Pharaoh and his great host: not a single man of their many thousands came back with them to their lands.
After their condemnation, a firm deed, after the killing of their firstborn, as no sage conceals, in ordered lines, they let them go with all they had. They let them go free from them.
The King who brought the race of Israel out, when the great choir praised him: not counting women and boys, six hundred thousand armed men fit for battle.
Then they reached land and gave thanks to the high king for their escape from the danger of captivity, after the drowning of their bitter enemies.
After that the choir was raised in praise of God, as was fitting. They sang, and godly was its strength, “[?] Let us sing!”
Then Moses' sister, great Miriam, played the timbrel; with the women of the sons of Israel she sang music to the King of the clouds.

The glorious King who split before the host the ridges of the dark-red [?] sea; the King above every power, with the heaven of the clouds; the King who brought the race of Israel. The King brought the race of Israel out.
They were thankful to steadfast God after escaping from the Red Sea, but they were soon displeased with God when they came into the wilderness.
“Alas that God has brought us into this hardship [?] and did not leave us in Egypt. He has led us along paths of every kind to our deaths in the wilderness.
“Without food, without drink, a great wrong, without clothing too, forever naked: poverty has filled us, death has come upon us, famine will kill us.”
The King, renowned in his ways, said to them: “While you are in the wilderness, you will not suffer, out of doors or in the house, any lack of food or clothing.”
The King who fed them with soft manna and a flock of tender birds; the water for their help, from every plain, he brought them out of the rock.
The streams of the wilderness, a fitting sound, though they were deadly poison for everyone, and bitter and [?], to them were sweet to taste.
They made their way, a victorious company, with the great bright sea on their left hand, north-west across every wood [?], into the territory of fierce Amalek.
They fought fierce, bloody battles against the dreadful host of Amalek; many armed men fell there through the cross-vigil of Moses.
When they had slaughtered the host of renowned, hardy Amalek, they pitched their camp in silent ranks about Mount Sinai.
After battles and champions' fights against the wrathful race of Amalek, on Mount Sinai, mighty as a host in valour, they were in triumphant deeds. They were thankful to steadfast God.
A wondrous thing appeared to them at once on Mount Sinai before the face of the host, with bright thunder: a great red fiery flame.
He who came from heaven, from the strongholds of star-bright heaven, so that he laid down a whole and especially wise law for the renowned race of Abraham.
The King who called Moses, fair in his deeds, to him on Mount Sinai, without drink, without food, a bright course, to the end of forty days.
The King who gave Moses ten pure words of wisdom, in ordered rules, a dear course, to instruct the great people.
To give a plain law, without error, through his pure sense, the King came from green heaven with commandments for them. It appeared. A wondrous thing appeared to them.
While Moses was on the mountain, [?], a calf of choice red gold was made by them. It was no right deed.
Then, worse than any tale, the tribes of the sons of Israel, both men and women, without grace, all went to worship it.
To renounce the pure King of angels was a great crime for the great host, and the image of a lifeless calf eating rough grass.
God was justly angry with them, with the deceitful race of Jacob, so that he very nearly cast the host beneath the earth in one moment.
Then Moses prayed to the King with his angels that their correction and restraint be left to him, at his own full discretion.
Were it not for Moses, of bright bearing, said the King who orders all, he would not leave one man of them alive on earth, for all their fighting and valour.
Before the face of God, a godly searching, learning the rule and the royal mystery, on Mount Sinai, a bright track, long was Moses there. While Moses was on the mountain.
Moses strongly commanded the host that was with him then that for the space of three hours they should slay the great host.
No one was to spare, a bloody cry, his mother or his father, or his brother, of famous boast, or his beloved or his friend.
Moses slew, a bright deed, both beast and man, men and boys and women; he put them under the sword of vengeance.
Then he ground to powder the firm image of red gold and gave it to the great host in their food. That was no pity.
God commanded, with bright thunder, his correction, without a trace of mercy, by the order of wisdom, a bloody constraint; it was Moses he charged with it. Moses strongly commanded.
A grim plague came upon them some time later, a disease of the bowels; many of the host died of the very red, bloody flux.
The King said to them plainly: “Make a bronze serpent. Let it be raised up with grace on a tree above the host, to be gazed upon.
“Whoever on the plain looks at the tree and the serpent will be whole, whatever they do; they will not die of the disease.”
It speaks there of a figure of Christ, who came to save us, who was raised with grace upon a tree: it was for our sake that he was crucified.
Whoever looks there upon Jesus Christ, adorned above all, will have heaven, a firm bond, in everlasting union with the archangels.
The hosts of the seed of Adam from every place, both saints and sinners, many, all of them, of bright and equal rank, are in company with Moses.

Were it not for the King of noble heaven, who has power over all, of good grace, there would have been a multitude of horrors from every quarter upon the peoples it reached. A grim plague came upon them.
The King spoke to them without grief, to the wondrous children of Israel, that they should make for themselves a pure church and the Ark of the Testimony.
Two men were theirs to undertake the hewing, the craftsmanship and the master smithwork: Adiar, skilled and of high dignity, and the wondrous Ithidun.
From the tribe of Levi, a dear company, by the will of the King of the saints, came seventy men, a goodly band, to help them and to serve.
The first work they made was a great laver, a bronze vat in its place, with many figures and a broad form, a very sea, the measure of thirteen men.
The second work shows a mystery, as the Scripture relates: among men and boys and women, an iron hook [?] for every single man after that.
The third work, bright and faultless, was the house of God, the tabernacle. It was no trifle to dear God, with its thousands of wonders.
The fourth work was the pure Ark, fair to carry on every march, of gleaming gold, a shelter to every tribe, like every richly shaped shrine.
The King measured out for them (it was a triumph) the great, holy and pure church: its length, without falsehood, its height and its breadth.
Thirty cubits, a bright joining, were its breadth and its height; fifty cubits, a fine form [?], was its length as it was set.
It was made of fair boards, pure in form, sound, noble and shapely, every piece of choice, precious shittim wood cut to plan.
It was a four-cornered enclosure, a building of ranks, not huge or ill-shaped, with bright walls, a perfect work, and splendid gilded panels [?].
The King set the boards in poles [?] and placed them in rows of noble rank; he divided them with skilful joints: seventy-two stately boards.
Twelve boards around the strong door, a fair measure without excess; fourteen boards, that is certain, are ranged around the window.
Twenty-three boards on each side are fitted without fear and without error; two cubits (I will not hide it in the east) was the breadth of each board.
Four boards at the two ends [?], in the corners of the church; as was measured (a royal word), there were thirty cubits in each board.
Sixteen bases, sure and faultless, of seven score [of silver], were beneath them on the floor (a festive sight): two bases under each board.
The height of the tenons [?] below, above the bases of white bronze: a cubit was the length of each hand, without excess of measure.
A door straight to the east, stately and princely, bright toward the sun, fair and full, a work without ugliness, every form lasting; the sanctuary was at its very western end.
Four full boards, a bright work, held up the sanctuary, with bases before the tribes and with gilded figures.
An altar by the door on the north, for burning holy, pure offerings; an altar made ready on the south, for the prayers of the faithful.
The chief altar with its grace, for whose noble work glory was raised up, every part with borders of gold; it was as high as Aaron's breast.
A [?] in the west within, its [?] like bright purple; every [?] straight and solid, to raise up the ridge-poles.
Strong, straight pillars from the floor, for setting up [?] of noble rank, under the swift, sure ridge-pole of the host, with thirteen figures of red gold.
A column [?] through the strong ridge-pole, for fastening the ropes; upon it above, without grief (a fitting lay), a noble bird with a golden face.
So that they reached the floor on either side over the boards in an even row: hangings of many-coloured linen made to stretch out from the ridge-pole.
One cloth over them on the outside, fairly they came [?], though they were strong, against wasting [?] rains, against the heavens, against rough winds.
A clasp of silver, bright and unfailing, on each of the two chief halves, by fastenings, a choice [?], seventy loops of red gold.
As a cord for them, as a bright fastening for the true, joined linen cloths, a firm hook of choice red gold was to be put on every single loop.
It is set over them outside, to be seen by the hosts, sides [?] for the eyes of the host, thirteen [?] of red gold.
'Make, for the benefit of every company, a wondrous Ark (sure the pledge [?]) for the rod, for the manna, for the bright gold, for the inscribed tablets.'
Four cubits, a bright measure, were to be the length of the Ark; three its height, a right measure, and two its breadth.
Four rings of solid gold on the Ark, for carrying it; two poles through them, red in their look, of wondrous refined gold.
Figures of cherubim upon the Ark, of gold of great beauty around it, with lustrous [?], bright [?], with the shade of their outspread wings.
In the sanctuary let the holy Ark be placed by you with its instruments, and a curtain of silk, a row without [?], between the host and the sanctuary.
With sun-bright songs of every kind, with choirs, with music, with prayers, with choruses, with great praises.
The rod of Moses, the rod of keen Aaron, without weakness, with [?] of great grace: fifty ounces of bright, pure gold in each of those two rods.
The good rod of Moses, a right work, which brought its plagues on Egypt: a shaped serpent, gleaming in form, was set firmly at its top.
The rod of Aaron, a wondrous treasure, of pure, glorious grace before the shining face, with goodly blossom of holy fragrance, bearing the fruit of every good thing.

through his fierce fury of deadly strength [?]

With hosts, with peoples, with desires of strongholds [?],

Joab made for the noble king

When Joab was sent, a sad tale.

The Lord was angry with him, a fresh burden.

fire burned both [offerings]

the bright oil, clear with grace —
